question: A 43-year-old woman visits her primary care provider complaining of fatigue. Although she has had it for several months, her fatigue has been worsening over the past few weeks. She has no other symptoms. Past medical history is significant for hypertension. She takes chlorthalidone, an oral contraceptive pill, and a multivitamin every day. Family history is noncontributory. She drinks about 1 bottle of wine every day and started taking a shot or two of whisky or vodka every morning before work to “clear out the cobwebs”. She was recently fired from her job. Today, her heart rate is 90/min, respiratory rate is 17/min, blood pressure is 110/65 mm Hg, and temperature is 36.7°C (98.1°F). On physical exam, she appears malnourished and anxious. Her conjunctiva are pale, and glossitis is noted on oral exam. Her heart has a regular rate and rhythm and her lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. She has no gait or balance abnormalities. Lab results show a hemoglobin of 10 g/dL, with a mean corpuscular volume (MCV) of 108 fl. Elevated level of which of the following will most likely to be found in this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Fatigue and glossitis" -> "Macrocytic anemia" -> "Elevated MCV" -> "Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency" -> "Elevated homocysteine" -> 85%
CHAIN: "Fatigue and glossitis" -> "Macrocytic anemia" -> "Elevated MCV" -> "Vitamin B12 deficiency" -> "Elevated methylmalonic acid" -> 75%
CHAIN: "Fatigue and glossitis" -> "Macrocytic anemia" -> "Elevated MCV" -> "Alcohol use" -> "Folate deficiency" -> "Elevated homocysteine" -> 80%
CHAIN: "Fatigue and glossitis" -> "Macrocytic anemia" -> "Elevated MCV" -> "Alcohol use" -> "Possible vitamin B12 deficiency" -> "Elevated methylmalonic acid" -> 70%
CHAIN: "Fatigue and glossitis" -> "Macrocytic anemia" -> "Elevated MCV" -> "Alcohol use" -> "Possible folate deficiency" -> "Elevated homocysteine" -> 75%
enhanced_information: The patient presents with fatigue, glossitis, and macrocytic anemia, indicated by an elevated MCV of 108 fl. These symptoms are consistent with either vitamin B12 or folate deficiency. Given her alcohol use, folate deficiency is more likely, as alcohol interferes with folate metabolism. Both vitamin B12 and folate deficiencies can lead to elevated homocysteine levels. However, only vitamin B12 deficiency leads to elevated methylmalonic acid levels. The presence of glossitis and macrocytic anemia, along with her alcohol consumption, suggests a higher likelihood of folate deficiency, which would result in elevated homocysteine levels. Therefore, the most likely elevated substance in this patient is homocysteine. The retrieved evidence paths broadly support the link between fatigue and macrocytic anemia but do not specifically address the distinction between vitamin B12 and folate deficiencies. Thus, the best consensus-supported interpretation is that homocysteine is elevated due to folate deficiency exacerbated by alcohol use.
analysis: The patient presents with symptoms and lab findings consistent with macrocytic anemia, specifically an elevated MCV, fatigue, glossitis, and pale conjunctiva. These are indicative of either vitamin B12 or folate deficiency. Given her significant alcohol consumption, folate deficiency is more likely, as alcohol can interfere with folate absorption and metabolism. Both vitamin B12 and folate deficiencies can lead to elevated homocysteine levels, but only vitamin B12 deficiency results in elevated methylmalonic acid levels. The absence of neurological symptoms, which are more common in vitamin B12 deficiency, and the presence of alcohol use, which is more commonly associated with folate deficiency, suggest that folate deficiency is the more likely cause. Therefore, the most likely elevated substance in this patient is homocysteine, which is elevated in both deficiencies but more indicative of folate deficiency in this context.
